name: THE THAT GIRL IS HOISIN BURGER (Comes with blue cheese)

recipe.history:
Hoisin sauce — known in Cantonese as hoisin jeung, meaning loosely "seafood sauce" despite containing no seafood — is a fermented condiment with deep roots in Chinese culinary tradition, believed to have originated in southern China, particularly in the Cantonese-speaking regions of Guangdong province. Its primary base is fermented soybean paste, combined with garlic, sesame, five spice, and various sweeteners, and the result is a sauce of extraordinary complexity: deeply sweet, funky from fermentation, fragrant with anise and fennel from the five spice blend, and with a thickness and richness that coats everything it touches. Hoisin appears in Chinese cuisine as a dipping sauce for Peking duck, where it is spread inside a thin pancake with scallions and cucumber before the crispy duck is added — a preparation that is one of the most harmonious flavor combinations in world cooking. It is also a key component in moo shu pork, in various noodle preparations, and as a glaze for barbecued meats.

Hoisin's path into Western kitchens ran through Chinese-American restaurants and then through the broader adoption of Asian pantry staples that accelerated in the 1990s and 2000s. American food writers who had discovered Peking duck developed a taste for hoisin as a general-purpose glaze and condiment, and fusion chefs began incorporating it into non-Chinese preparations — hoisin barbecue sauce, hoisin-glazed ribs, hoisin vinaigrette for salads. The hoisin burger emerged naturally from this tradition, particularly in cities with strong Chinese-American food cultures. The sauce behaves similarly to a teriyaki glaze — it caramelizes on a hot surface, forms a lacquered crust, and adds sweetness balanced by deep umami — but its flavor profile is more complex and its fermented character gives it a depth that teriyaki lacks. The addition of blue cheese in this burger is an inspired counterintuitive pairing: the funk and sharpness of aged Gorgonzola or Roquefort meets the sweet-savory complexity of hoisin across a medium rare patty, and the contrast creates something greater than either ingredient alone.

I first tried hoisin on a burger at a small counter in San Francisco's Richmond District that had no printed menu and operated on the principle that you got what the cook felt like making. The burger arrived wrapped in white paper, hoisin-glazed and dripping, with a smear of blue cheese that I hadn't expected. My first instinct was skepticism — the combination seemed designed to provoke rather than to please. My second instinct, which came about three bites in, was that the person who invented this deserved some kind of recognition. The sweet funk of the hoisin and the sharp, pungent blue cheese were arguing with each other in the most productive way imaginable, and the medium rare beef was the peacemaker that made both flavors coherent. I asked the cook how he came up with it and he said he just had both in the refrigerator one night and thought, why not.

There is wisdom in the "why not" school of cooking, but it requires that the underlying technique be sound — and in this case, the underlying technique is a patty cooked to exactly medium rare, 130–135°F. The hoisin glaze caramelizes on the exterior of the patty in the last moments of cooking, and if the patty is overcooked the interior will be dry and the glaze will be the only thing providing any moisture or flavor. At medium rare, the glaze is an additional layer of complexity, not a compensatory measure. The blue cheese melts partially over the hot crust and stays partially crumbled — the contrast of textures and temperatures within the cheese itself mirrors the contrast between the sweet-funky hoisin and the sharp dairy tang. This is a burger that requires precision to work.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
4 scallions, thinly sliced on the diagonal
½ English cucumber, halved lengthwise, seeded, and thinly sliced
instructions: 1. MAKE THE BUNS — Combine flour, yeast, sugar, and salt in a stand mixer bowl.
2. Add warm milk, warm water, egg, and butter. Mix with dough hook on low until combined, then medium speed for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic.
3. Cover and let rise until doubled, about 1 hour.
4. Divide into 4 portions, shape into balls, place on a lined sheet pan, flatten. Cover and proof 45 minutes.
5. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush with egg wash and sprinkle with sesame seeds. Bake 16–18 minutes until golden. Cool on a rack.
6. MAKE THE HOISIN GLAZE — Combine hoisin sauce, soy sauce, rice vinegar, honey, garlic, ginger, and sesame oil in a small saucepan over medium-low heat.
7. Stir and simmer 3–4 minutes until slightly thickened. Set aside. Divide into two portions: one for glazing the patties, one for the bun.
8. MAKE THE SCALLION-CUCUMBER SLAW — Toss scallions and cucumber with rice vinegar, sesame oil, honey, and a pinch of salt. Let sit at room temperature 15 minutes.
9. MAKE THE SRIRACHA MAYO — Stir together mayonnaise and Sriracha if using. Set aside.

10. FORM THE PATTIES — Divide beef into 4 equal portions (about 170g each). Form into patties ¾-inch thick with a thumb dimple in the center. Season both sides with salt, pepper, and garlic powder just before cooking.
11. COOK THE PATTIES — Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat with a thin film of neutral oil until smoking.
12. Cook patties undisturbed for 3 minutes until a deep brown crust forms. Flip once.
13. Immediately brush the cooked side with hoisin glaze. Scatter blue cheese crumbles generously over the glazed side.
14. Cook 2–2½ more minutes. In the last 30 seconds, brush the underside of each patty with glaze by pressing the brush under the edge of the patty.
15. Check internal temperature — target 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare.
16. Remove and tent with foil. Rest 3 minutes while the blue cheese softens into the glaze.
17. TOAST THE BUNS — Split buns and toast cut-side down in the pan over medium heat, 60–90 seconds.
18. ASSEMBLE — Brush the cut side of each bottom bun with remaining hoisin glaze.
19. Spread Sriracha mayo on the top bun.
20. Place a butter lettuce leaf on the bottom bun.
21. Set the hoisin-glazed, blue cheese-topped patty on the lettuce.
22. Pile the scallion-cucumber slaw on top of the blue cheese.
23. Cap with the top bun and serve immediately.
